explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. John says many of the Jews who had come to Mary, and had seen what Jesus did, believed in Him (John 11:45). They didn't just watch a dead man walk out of the tomb and shrug (John 11:44). Believing is where this whole passage starts, and it's the part I like best.

Not this time, friend. John says plainly that many of the Jews who had come to Mary, and had seen what Jesus did, believed in Him (John 11:45). Some of them did go off and tell the Pharisees, but that's the next verse (John 11:46). Verse 45 says many believed.
That's it, baker. The council says, "This man is performing many signs." (John 11:47) Notice what they don't say. They don't argue that the signs didn't happen. I think that has them worried.

Sabbath trouble does come up with Jesus in other places, like John 5:16, but not in this verse. Here the council asks, "What are we to do?" and then says, "This man is performing many signs." (John 11:47) The signs are what they name about Jesus in this meeting. The Sabbath never comes up.

Good guess for a council meeting, but it's not what they say. Their words are, "This man is performing many signs." (John 11:47) Moses never comes up in this passage. The signs are what they name about Jesus here.

Right, friend. The council says, "…everyone will believe in Him, and then the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation." (John 11:48) That's what they say they're afraid of. The Romans were the empire that ruled the land back then (Luke 3:1).

The Greeks are a fair guess, but the council doesn't name them. They say, "…then the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation." (John 11:48) Romans were the empire that ruled the land back then (Luke 3:1). The council's worry is about them.

Egypt shows up all over the Bible, but not in this verse. The council says, "…then the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation." (John 11:48) The Romans were the empire in charge at this time (Luke 3:1). That's who the council has on its mind.

That's the word, baker. Caiaphas says, "…it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish." (John 11:50) He's the high priest that year, and that's what he tells the room. John explains right after that there's more going on in those words than Caiaphas said himself.

I see why you'd pick it, since this whole meeting is a lot of talking. But Caiaphas says it's better that one man "die" for the people (John 11:50). Speaking isn't what he has in mind. His point is that one man's death is better than the whole nation perishing.

Prayer is a kind thought, friend, but it's not what Caiaphas says. His words are, "…it is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish." (John 11:50) The word is "die," and it's a heavy one. I think that's why it sticks.

Yes, baker! John says Jesus would die "…to gather them together into one." (John 11:52) Scattered children, brought together. I came out of a junk drawer, so a gathering like that gets me right in the apron.

explanations.answer: Make them priests in the temple
explanations.explanation: Close to the temple, but that's not what John says. Jesus would die for the scattered children of God "…to gather them together into one." (John 11:52) Priests aren't mentioned in that verse. The gathering is the point.

explanations.answer: Set them free from the Romans
explanations.explanation: The Romans do come up back in verse 48, but not like this. There the council says they're afraid the Romans "…will come and take away both our place and our nation." (John 11:48) Here, Jesus would die for the scattered children of God "…to gather them together into one." (John 11:52) John doesn't mention freeing anyone from the Romans in this verse.

That's the word, friend. John says, "So from that day on they plotted to kill Him." (John 11:53) It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to just say so. The plotting starts the very day Caiaphas speaks.
Banishing sounds like a gentler plan, but it's not what John says. "So from that day on they plotted to kill Him." (John 11:53) It's a heavy verse. The word is kill.

Discrediting someone is a slower, quieter plan, but that's not what the text says. John writes, "So from that day on they plotted to kill Him." (John 11:53) It's a heavy verse, so I'll just say it plainly. The plot is to kill.

That's the one, baker. Jesus withdrew "…to a town called Ephraim in an area near the wilderness. And He stayed there with the disciples." (John 11:54) John says that's the result of the plot, so Jesus stepped out of public view.

Emmaus is a real town in the Gospels, but it's not this one. John says Jesus withdrew "…to a town called Ephraim in an area near the wilderness." (John 11:54) Emmaus comes up in a different story (Luke 24:13). Here it's Ephraim.

Bethsaida is a town you'll meet elsewhere in the Gospels, like in Mark 8:22. But this verse says Jesus withdrew "…to a town called Ephraim in an area near the wilderness." (John 11:54) He stayed there with the disciples. Bethsaida isn't part of this passage.

Not quite, friend. The people are asking each other, "What do you think? Will He come to the feast at all?" (John 11:56) That sounds like wondering to me, not being sure. I think they really couldn't say.

Right, baker. The crowds in the temple courts were asking each other, "What do you think? Will He come to the feast at all?" (John 11:56) That's a question, not a promise. They kept looking for Him, and I think they couldn't say for sure what He'd do.

explanations.answer: Anyone who knows where He is must report it
explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. John says the chief priests and Pharisees "…had given orders that anyone who knew where He was must report it, so that they could arrest Him." (John 11:57) The plot from verse 53 is turning into actual orders. It's a heavy end to the passage.

explanations.answer: Anyone who follows Him must leave the city
explanations.explanation: That would be a different kind of order, and John doesn't say it. The leaders ordered "…that anyone who knew where He was must report it, so that they could arrest Him." (John 11:57) The order is about reporting where He is. It doesn't mention followers leaving.

explanations.answer: No one may say His name in the temple
explanations.explanation: Interesting guess, but it's not in the text. John says the orders were "…that anyone who knew where He was must report it, so that they could arrest Him." (John 11:57) The crowds were still talking about Him in the temple courts (John 11:56). The order is about reporting where He is.
